newsitem.title: USA: U.S. must be firm in Japan air talks - Northwest CEO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. must be firm in Japan air talks - Northwest CEO.

text.p: The United States should settle for nothing less than an "open skies" agreement with Japan that would provide unrestricted access to each other's air service markets, the top executive of Northwest Airlines Corp. said Thursday.

"We should stand firm for open skies," Northwest Chief Executive Officer John Dasburg told a House panel. "The alternative, amending the current agreement as Japan urges, would be a resounding trade defeat."

In prepared testimony to the House aviation subcommittee, Dasburg said that if it were not for the competitive advantage U.S. airlines have over Japanese carriers, the $48 billion U.S. trade deficit with Japan would be even bigger.
"If not for U.S. carriers who are winning the competitive war with Japanese carriers, that annual drain on the U.S. economy would be more than $5 billion greater," he said.
Settling for less than an open skies agreement will also harm the U.S. trade balance throughout Asia, he said.
He complained that under the "managed trade" proposals being considered by both countries, U.S. carriers would lose flexibility in servicing the lucrative Asian market.

"I believe it would be a trade mistake of colossal proportions if we were to let our carriers be relegated to the future role of transPacific feeder service for Japanese carriers serving the rest of Asia," he added.
But Gerald Greenwald, chairman and chief executive officer of UAL Corp's United Airlines, told the subcommittee that U.S. negotiators needed to be pragmatic.
"I submit that it is time for U.S. aviation relations with Japan to be result-oriented and for our negotiating strategy to be based on pragmatism," he said in prepared testimony to the subcommittee.

"What we need, and what United believes can be negotiated, is an interim agreement that, while other than 'open skies,' can produce benefits of the magnitude generated by our bilateral with Canada," Greenwald said.
The United States and Canada signed an agreement in 1995 to liberalize air service between the two countries.
The United States and Japan have been engaged in talks for the past year to try to resolve problems in their current 1952 bilateral treaty and expand rights between the two countries.
The Japanese government has proposed unlimited aviation rights for two Japanese carriers -- Japan Airlines Co Ltd and All Nippon Airways Co Ltd -- and two U.S. carriers -- Northwest and United.

"This position serves Japan's interests well since Japan's international airline industry consists of basically only two airlines ...," U.S. Assistant Secretary of Transportation told the panel in prepared testimony.
"This approach would esentially give Japan's international airline industry unrestricted access to the U.S. market while excluding a major portion of the U.S. industry from liberal access to Japan."
